content.text: How can charged objects exert forces on each other without touching? The answer lies in electric fields—invisible regions of influence that surround every charged object. Understanding electric fields helps explain phenomena from static electricity to how electrons move in circuits and how particle accelerators work.
An electric field is a region around a charged object where another charged object would experience a force. Field lines point away from positive charges and towards negative charges.

Particle accelerators such as CERN's Large Hadron Collider use powerful electric fields to accelerate charged particles to near light speed, enabling physicists to study the fundamental building blocks of matter.
"Field lines are the paths charges follow"
— Field lines show the direction of force, not necessarily the path. A moving charge may curve due to its velocity.
"Electric fields only exist between charged objects"
— A single charged object has a field around it, regardless of whether other charges are present.
"The field is zero where there are no field lines"
— We only draw a selection of lines. The field exists everywhere, not just on the drawn lines.
— Only the field between parallel plates is uniform. Fields around point charges get weaker with distance.
"Positive charges create stronger fields than negative charges"
— Equal magnitude charges create equal strength fields; only the direction differs.
Electric field: region where charged objects experience a force
Field direction: direction a positive charge would move
Field lines: away from positive, towards negative, never cross
